title: Sh-Ch-R
hookLine: shachar, dawn; Shacharit, the morning prayer

lines: LET ME GO, FOR THE DAY BREAKETH.
cards: All night, beside a river, Jacob wrestles with a stranger. The stranger can't overcome him. Jacob is hurt, but he won't let go.
Then the stranger says, "Let me go, for the day breaketh." In Hebrew, ki alah ha-shachar: for the dawn has come up. And Jacob answers, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."
The night is ending, and the first light is the thing the stranger can't stay for. Today's root is the word for that light.

teach.b: Sh-Ch-R. Shin, chet, resh. Shachar: dawn, the first light.
First, a psalm that gets up before the sun: "Awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early." The Hebrew is a'irah shachar, which can also be read: I will wake the dawn.
Not waiting for morning to wake you; going out to wake it.

Second, another psalm asks where a person could go to get away from God's presence: "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me."
The wings of the morning are kanfei shachar, the dawn's wings. As far and as fast as light can run, and still held. Third, the prayer.
The morning service is Shacharit, the dawn prayer. The Talmud gives two views of where the daily prayers come from.
One says the patriarchs established them, and gives the morning to Abraham, from a verse: "Abraham gat up early in the morning to the place where he stood before the LORD."
The other ties the prayers to the daily offerings in the Temple. Fourth, the line itself.

teach.h: THE ROOSTER TELLS DAY FROM NIGHT.
teach.b: Among the morning blessings is one that thanks God for giving the rooster understanding to tell day from night.
Dawn is a line drawn slowly across the sky, and the tradition meets it with words.

how: Shacharit, the morning service, is prayed each day from dawn; it opens with the morning blessings, including thanks for the rooster's understanding to tell day from night, and the Talmud links it to Abraham rising early (Berakhot 26b).

games.q: you've wrestled a stranger all night by the river. you're hurt, and now he says, let me go, for the day breaketh. what do you do?
o: let go. you've survived the night.
hold on until he blesses you.
ask him to stay until noon.
games.why: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." the dawn is the thing the stranger can't stay for, and Jacob leaves with a blessing.

practice: If it's morning, turn toward a window; if it's later, find the brightest light near you, or close your eyes and remember the last sunrise you saw.

Look for the edge where light meets shadow, on a wall, the floor, the side of your hand, and watch it while your breathing slows. If you pray, you can say the psalm's words: I myself will awake early.

wordCard.voice: Sh-Ch-R. Shin, chet, resh: shachar, the dawn, and Shacharit, the prayer that meets it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: dawn, from shin, chet, resh; Shacharit, the morning prayer, comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: dawn. Even the rooster's good sense gets a blessing. Good morning, whenever it is.
